title: Permanent versus determinant
formal: Over \(\mathbb C\), is the determinantal complexity of the permanent not bounded above by any polynomial? Precisely, writing \(d_n=\operatorname{dc}_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)\) as defined below, is it true that for every triple of integers \(B,k,N\ge1\) there is an integer \(n\ge N\) with \(d_n>B(n+1)^k\)? The matrices in the definition are unrestricted exact affine-linear representations over \(\mathbb C\).
definitions: For an integer \(n\ge1\), let \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) consist of \(n^2\) algebraically independent commuting variables over \(\mathbb C\). Let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and set \(\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}\). For any \(m\times m\) matrix \(M\) over a commutative ring, \(\det(M)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{a=1}^m M_{a,\pi(a)}\), where \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{|\{(a,b):a<b,\ \pi(a)>\pi(b)\}|}\). Define \(d_n\) to be the least integer \(m\ge1\) for which there exist constant matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}\), one \(A_{ij}\) for each input variable, such that \[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\det\!\left(A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}A_{ij}\right)\] as an identity in \(\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]\). Thus every entry is a constant plus an arbitrary complex linear combination of all input variables. Equality means equality of every coefficient, equivalently equality for every complex assignment, not just Boolean assignments. Finite representations exist, so the minimum is defined; for example the known bound \(d_n\le2^n-1\) suffices. The resource is the matrix dimension \(m\), not its number of entries, coefficient bit lengths or time to find the matrices. Constants can be arbitrary complex numbers, independently for each \(n\), with no computability or uniform construction requirement. Variables may be reused in any number of entries. No symmetry, sparsity, rank condition on \(A_0\), sign restriction, read-once property or restriction on cancellation is imposed. A limit of determinants is not an exact representation unless some permitted matrix already has determinant equal to the permanent. Since every \(d_n\) is finite, the formal assertion is equivalent to nonexistence of integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfying \(d_n\le B(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\ge1\): finitely many exceptions to an upper bound can be absorbed into \(B\). The stated lower-bound quantifiers require arbitrarily large violating indices for every proposed polynomial, not eventual domination of that polynomial at every sufficiently large index.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified lower-bound proposition, or of its logical negation: there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) there exist an integer \(1\le m\le B(n+1)^k\) and complex matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\) satisfying the exact polynomial identity above. A negative answer may prove existence of this nonuniform family without an algorithm to generate its constants. A positive answer must exclude all allowed affine-linear matrices for the relevant \(n,m\), including those that break the permanent’s symmetries. A fixed-degree polynomial lower bound, a bound restricted to real coefficients or a restricted matrix class, or a lower bound for a different polynomial does not prove the proposition. A polynomial-size limiting representation alone does not refute this exact target.
why: The permanent and determinant have almost identical permutation formulas, but the determinant is a basic efficiently computable polynomial whereas the permanent encodes algebraic counting. This conjecture asks whether enlarging the matrix and changing all its entries to affine forms can bridge that difference at polynomial cost. A superpolynomial lower bound would exclude an entire central model of algebraic computation, including polynomial-size algebraic branching programs and formulas.

importance.reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.

progress.text: Valiant’s framework supplies finite determinantal representations, efficient simulation of formulas and branching programs, and completeness of the permanent for algebraic counting; the inspected 2021 source explains the distinction from unrestricted VP lower bounds.
Mignon and Ressayre’s Theorem 2 gives the characteristic-zero lower bound \(d_n\ge n^2/2\). The author manuscript’s statement and definitions were visually inspected.

Grenet’s exponential-size construction is recorded and shown optimal under left permutation/diagonal symmetry in Landsberg and Ressayre’s Theorem 2.8. The inspected preprint is from August 2015; the journal publication is from 2017.
Kumar and Volk’s Theorem 1 improves the lower bound for the different polynomial \(\sum_i x_i^n\), while their introduction retains the permanent’s quadratic-versus-exponential gap.

The Algebraic Cost of a Boolean Sum separates the permanent and determinant under a uniform fixed additive cost for simple projections after shared-bit summation. This does not establish a general superpolynomial determinantal lower bound.

Bogart and Valero’s journal article studies two generalized permanent families; its introduction continues to identify the unrestricted ordinary-permanent question as open. The available publisher text and full 2022 preprint introduction were checked.

Sheshadri’s preprint claims a quadratic border bound for diagonal power sums. The inspected Theorem 1 concerns a different family, and its proof was not independently checked. Version 1 remains the sole arXiv version on 14 September.

status_note: The exact unrestricted complex-field question remains open in the inspected December 2025 paper and May 2026 Bogart–Valero journal introduction. Bounded searches through 14 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The June 2026 border claim concerns diagonal power sums, and its proof was not independently verified. Symmetry restrictions, real-field bounds, border upper bounds and Boolean-sum simple projections are not substituted for this card’s exact model.

context_blocks.text: The determinant attaches a permutation sign to each product that the permanent sums without signs. Simply changing signs on the original \(n\times n\) matrix is a very special representation; this card permits arbitrarily larger matrices and arbitrary affine entries. Its size parameter is \(n\), while the number of independent input variables is \(n^2\). Polynomial boundedness in either parameter is equivalent, but the distinction matters when describing a quadratic lower bound.

An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a source and sink, whose edges carry affine-linear forms; it computes the sum, over source-to-sink paths, of the products of their edge labels. Polynomial-size branching programs and polynomial-size determinantal representations simulate each other with polynomial overhead. General arithmetic circuits are directed acyclic computations using addition and multiplication and may reuse earlier results more freely. The algebraic class \(\mathrm{VP}\) permits polynomial-size circuits for families with polynomially bounded degree and number of variables; \(\mathrm{VNP}\) additionally permits summation over polynomially many Boolean variables. The permanent is complete for \(\mathrm{VNP}\). A polynomial-size determinant family for it would imply \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VNP}\), but the requested superpolynomial determinant lower bound by itself is not a separation from every unrestricted arithmetic circuit.

Mignon and Ressayre’s characteristic-zero theorem gives \(d_n\ge n^2/2\), while Grenet’s construction gives \(d_n\le2^n-1\). The quadratic lower bound is only linear in the permanent’s \(n^2\) variables and falls short of excluding every polynomial. The 2026 Bogart–Valero introduction still presents a quadratic-versus-exponential gap for the ordinary permanent; its new bounds concern generalized permanent families. Historical or recent bounds for another polynomial are not automatically permanent bounds.

Landsberg and Ressayre’s Theorem 2.8 proves the \(2^n-1\) lower bound for \(n\ge3\) when a representation respects the action of left multiplication by permutation and invertible diagonal matrices, and Grenet’s construction meets it. This theorem restricts how symmetries of the input polynomial lift to the representation. It imposes more than the exact identity defining \(d_n\). No symmetry requirement of this kind is part of the question.

Orzel and coauthors define a Boolean sum by first identifying all selected variable positions with one new variable \(y\), then adding the results for \(y=0\) and \(y=1\). This is a two-term sum, even when two positions are selected. Their Theorem 6 proves that for at most two selected positions the permanent can absorb this operation through a simple projection with dimension increased by at most three, while no fixed additive dimension increase works uniformly for the determinant. A simple projection substitutes constants or individual variables and uses each surviving variable at most once, allowing a nonzero overall scalar. This restricted, constant-additive-cost distinction leaves the unrestricted polynomial-size affine representations in this card open.

Border determinantal complexity also admits coefficientwise limits of fixed-dimension determinant representations; their matrix coefficients may vary and become unbounded along the limit. It is at most exact determinantal complexity. Thus a border lower bound implies the same exact lower bound, while an exact lower bound does not automatically exclude limiting representations. Changing the coefficient field also changes the model: allowing \(\mathbb C\) can reduce complexity compared with \(\mathbb R\), and in characteristic two the permanent equals the determinant. These variants cannot silently replace the fixed complex-field target.

Sheshadri’s June 2026 preprint claims a quadratic border lower bound for the diagonal power sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^n\). That polynomial has \(n\) variables and is not the \(n\times n\) permanent. The inspected theorem therefore does not close this card’s gap, regardless of its stronger dependence on the number of variables. The preprint proof has not been independently verified here.

sentences: The permanent sums permutation products without the signs used by the determinant.
The question asks whether its representation as a determinant of affine-linear forms can be bounded in dimension by any polynomial in the original matrix size.
Every complex coefficient and every reuse of input variables is allowed, with no symmetry or uniform construction requirement.
A superpolynomial lower bound would exclude polynomial-size algebraic branching programs and formulas for the permanent, while a polynomial-size representation would collapse VP and VNP.

A complete Lean proof must establish nonexistence of every polynomial bound or prove a polynomial-size exact family; restricted symmetry bounds, limiting representations and results for other polynomials do not settle this target.
